This vignette is closely related to the more general [FIMS diagnostics vignette](https://noaa-fims.github.io/FIMS/articles/fims-diagnostics.html)

The objective of this vignette is to demonstrate the use of Pearson residuals, using the information returned by `get_estimates()`. One-step-ahead (OSA) residuals (Waagepetersen 2006; Thygesen et al. 2017) and extensions are not yet available in FIMS.

This example uses the precomputed estimates for the package's `data_big` model, so it does not need to refit the model.

```{r setup}
library(FIMS)

data("estimates_big_optimized")
```

## Calculate Pearson residuals

A Pearson residual is calculated directly from the observed value minus the expected (fitted) value, divided by the square root of the model's variance (standard deviation). This calculation depends on the likelihood distribution -- for a lognormal likelihood (`log_normal` in FIMS) with meanlog $\mu$ and sdlog $\sigma$, the response-scale mean is $\exp(\mu + \sigma^2 / 2)$ and the variance is $\exp(2\mu + \sigma^2)(\exp(\sigma^2) - 1)$. FIMS reports `expected` as $\mu$ and `log_sd` as $\log(\sigma)$ for this likelihood.

The example below calculates response-scale Pearson residuals for the lognormal data streams.

```{r pearson-residuals}
lognormal_residuals <- estimates_big_optimized |>
  dplyr::filter(
    grepl("log_normal", tolower(.data$distribution))
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    sdlog = exp(.data$log_sd),
    expected_mean = exp(.data$expected + .data$sdlog^2 / 2),
    expected_variance = exp(2 * .data$expected + .data$sdlog^2) *
      (exp(.data$sdlog^2) - 1),
    pearson_residual = (.data$observed - .data$expected_mean) /
      sqrt(.data$expected_variance)
  ) 
```

Residuals near zero indicate observations close to the fitted expectation; large positive or negative values indicate observations that are poorly predicted under the assumed likelihood. 

## Plot residuals

`stockplotr::plot_timeseries()` provides the figure shown below. The example facets by stream label so that quantities from different data types are not mixed in a single panel. The year column in the estimates is an index (`year_i`)

```{r pearson-residual-plot}
residual_plot_data <- lognormal_residuals |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    year = .data$year_i,
    pearson_residual = .data$pearson_residual,
    model = "FIMS",
    group_var = .data$fleet
  )

stockplotr::plot_timeseries(
  residual_plot_data,
  x = "year",
  y = "pearson_residual",
  geom = "point",
  xlab = "Year index",
  ylab = "Pearson residual",
  group = "fleet",
  facet = "label"
) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  stockplotr::theme_noaa()
```

## Calculate Pearson residuals for multinomial likelihoods

For multinomial composition data, observations represent proportions across bins ($p_i$) with an effective sample size $N$. The expected value in bin $i$ is $p_i$ and the variance for category $i$ is $\frac{p_i(1 - p_i)}{N}$.

The Pearson residual for bin $i$ is:
$$r_i = \frac{o_i - p_i}{\sqrt{\frac{p_i(1 - p_i)}{N}}}$$

```{r multinomial-residuals}
multinomial_residuals <- estimates_big_optimized |>
  dplyr::filter(
    grepl("multinomial", tolower(.data$distribution))
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    expected_var = .data$expected * (1 - .data$expected),
    pearson_residual = dplyr::if_else(
      expected_var > 0,
      (.data$observed - .data$expected) / sqrt(expected_var),
      0
    )
  )

multinomial_residuals |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    year = .data$year_i,
    sign = ifelse(.data$pearson_residual >= 0, "Positive", "Negative")
  ) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = year, y = .data$age, size = abs(.data$pearson_residual), color = sign)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.05, 2.5), name = "Pearson residual") +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c("Positive" = "blue", "Negative" = "red")) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Year", y = "Age class", color = "Sign") +
  stockplotr::theme_noaa()

```
